title: Forms that do not feel like paperwork
metaTitle: Forms that feel like a conversation
excerpt: Group fields by the decision, say why you ask, and put the error next to the field. A form is a conversation with bad timing, so the questions have to carry the context.
alt: A laptop open to a code editor on a white desk, beside a plant and a yellow mug, a working desk for an article about forms that still feel human.
caption: A desk in the middle of the work, not a stack of forms. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: How should fields be grouped?
faqs.answer: Group them by the decision the person is making, such as who they are, what they want, and how to reach them. Three short groups with headings beat one long column of database fields. The heading can say why the group exists, in a clause, so the form does not feel like an interrogation.

faqs.question: Where should an error appear?
faqs.answer: Put the error in text beside the field, and keep everything they already typed. A red outline alone is not an explanation, and wiping the form punishes the one mistake. Move focus to the first problem so they can fix it and continue.

faqs.question: How is a checkout form different from a contact form?
faqs.answer: Checkout is where Baymard's compiled studies put average cart abandonment near 70 percent, much of it from people who were not ready to buy. The fields you can influence are the extra ones, the late surprise costs, and the errors that are hard to see. A contact form has the same manners, at lower stakes: ask less, explain why, and do not make them start over.

markdown:
Website form design is a conversation with bad timing. You ask everything before you can hear the answer, and you cannot nod, clarify, or skip ahead when they hesitate. Group the fields by the decision. Say why you ask. Put the error next to the field, in words. Those three habits are what keep a form from feeling like paperwork.

The person on the other side is busy and slightly suspicious. They will finish a short, legible set of questions. They will abandon a wall of fields that seems to serve your database more than their task.

## Group by the decision

Look at the form and name the decisions, not the columns. Who is this. What do they want. How should you reply. For checkout: what are they buying, where does it go, how will they pay. Each decision becomes a short group with a heading. The heading is a sentence fragment they can agree with before they type. "Where to send it" is human. "Shipping information" is a file drawer.

Three groups are usually enough. A fourth is a sign you are collecting a nice-to-have. Move nice-to-have out of the required path. You can ask on the next screen, or on the call, or never. Every required field is a claim that you cannot continue without it. If that claim is false, the field is a tax.

Order the groups the way a person would answer out loud. Identity, then the substance, then the logistics. Asking for a phone number before they have said what they need feels like the conversation already failed. On a demo request, the job they want to see comes before the company size. On a contact form, the message comes before a dropdown of departments, unless the department truly changes who answers.

[The W3C's WCAG overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) describes forms people can understand: labels, instructions, and errors that are programmatically and visually tied to the field. A heading over a group also helps, because it explains the relationship between the questions. Use a real legend or heading, not just a change in background color. Color is a hint. The words are the structure.

## Say why you ask

A reason in one clause disarms a field that would otherwise feel nosy. "Work email, so the invite does not bounce." "Order number, so we open the right shipment." "Company name, so we do not walk into the call blind." If you cannot write the clause, you do not need the field yet. Delete it. You can add it later when a real preparation task appears.

Put the reason where it remains visible, under the label or as part of the hint, not only as placeholder text. Placeholders vanish when people type, and they are a poor label for everyone. The label stays. The reason stays. The example, if you need one, is a hint, not the label itself.

Do not ask for data you will not use before you respond. A required "how did you hear about us" survey, sitting in front of a support request, tells the person their problem is less important than your attribution. Ask it later, optionally, or infer what you can from the page they were on. The form should feel like it is on their side of the task.

Legal checkboxes need the same honesty. Say what they are agreeing to, in the label, with the policy linked from meaningful words. A checkbox that says "I agree" and a tiny grey link is paperwork. A sentence they can read is a conversation, even when the law requires the tick. Keep it next to the action, in type that meets the same contrast as the rest of the form.

## Errors next to the field

When something is wrong, say what is wrong and how to fix it, beside the field. "Enter a work email so we can send the invite." "This card was declined. Try another, or check the number." A red border and a toast at the top of the page make people hunt. Some of them will not hunt. They will leave, and you will call it drop-off as if it were a mystery.

Keep their answers. Never clear a form on failure. The cost of retyping a message is enough to end the relationship before it starts. Move focus to the first error so keyboard users land on the problem. Summarize at the top only if there are several, and link each summary line to its field. The summary is a map. The repair happens at the field.

Do not rely on color. [WCAG's point about not using color alone](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) applies directly here. A red outline without text fails people who do not perceive that red, and it fails a screenshot pasted into a chat. The sentence has to travel. Icon plus color plus text is fine. Color alone is not.

Validate when it helps, not as a scold on every keystroke. An email field can wait until they leave it, or until they submit. A password rule can be visible before they type, as a checklist that updates, so the rules are not a surprise at the end. Surprise rules are paperwork. Visible rules are instructions, which is what you owed them at the start.

## Checkout is the form with a measured cost

Most forms on a marketing site are contact, signup, or demo. Checkout is the one researchers have counted carefully. [Baymard's compilation of cart studies](https://baymard.com/lists/cart-abandonment-rate), updated in 2025, puts the average documented abandonment rate at 70.22 percent across fifty studies. The same research is careful about cause. In Baymard's quantitative study, 42 percent of US online shoppers had abandoned because they were browsing or not ready to buy. That share is mostly out of the form's hands. The rest is where design works: extra fields, costs that appear late, accounts forced on guests, and errors that are hard to repair.

Treat that number as a ceiling full of window shopping, not as a verdict on your button color. Then remove the fields that are not needed to ship the order. Show shipping and tax before the card number. Let a guest finish when you do not truly need an account. Those moves are the same manners as a contact form, with money attached.

Down the Cove, as a public ecommerce migration and redesign, is a reminder that a shop's forms are part of the brand, not a template you tolerate at the end. The product page can be beautiful and the checkout can still feel like a different company. Same type, same tone, same refusal to ask twice. If you would not say the question out loud at the counter, do not put it in the form.

## The page around the fields

A form page still needs the promise. One sentence on what they will get after they submit. A demo agenda. A note that you reply within a business day, if that is true. The fields then make sense as the price of that outcome. A page that is only inputs assumes they have already decided, and many have not. Give them the decision in text beside the form, especially on a wide screen. On a phone, put it immediately above the first field, short enough to survive the scroll.

The button says what will happen. "Request the demo." "Send the message." "Pay 48 dollars." "Submit" says nothing. If there is a delay, say so on the button's neighbor, not in a disclaimer five screens back. After success, stay on a confirmation that repeats what happens next. Do not dump them on the homepage. Do not show an empty state that looks like the form failed.

Autocomplete is part of feeling human. Use the ordinary field purposes so browsers and phones can fill names and addresses. A custom control that looks like a text box and is not one will fight the tool that was trying to help. Fight the database's desire for special widgets. Use a native field unless you have a strong reason, and then test the strong reason with a keyboard and a phone.

Loading and errors from the network need a sentence too. "We could not send this. Your message is still here. Try again." Disable the button while the request is in flight so they do not double-submit, and say that you are sending it. A frozen button with no word is a different kind of paperwork, the kind that looks broken.

## A short review you can do this week

Print the form, or open it on a phone, and answer it yourself with real information. Count the required fields. For each, write the reason in the margin. Cross out any reason that is "we might want it later." Those fields leave.

Then break it on purpose. Empty submit. Bad email. Declined card, if you have a test card. Check that the message is next to the field and that your text survived. Turn on reduced motion and a screen reader if you can, or at least walk it with only the keyboard. The review is done when a tired person could finish it without asking you what a field means.

Watch the drop-off field if you have analytics that respect the people filling the form. The field where they leave is a question, not a moral failing. Either explain it, make it optional, or remove it. Changing the button color before you do that is how teams decorate a tax.

On a Hanabi build, forms are interface, designed in Figma with the groups and the errors present, then built in React and TypeScript so the messages and the focus behavior are part of the component. Tailwind keeps the error text in the same ramp as the body. The form should not look like a plugin from another brand. If it does, the conversation breaks at the exact moment you asked them to trust you with an email address.

## The limit of a friendly form

A kinder form will not create a reason to write to you. If the offer is unclear, shortening the form only speeds people to a conversation you are not ready to have. Fix the page that sent them. Then ask for the minimum. A short form in front of a vague promise collects leads you cannot serve, which is a different paperwork, done by your team after the submit.

A form also cannot replace a conversation that needs nuance. When the project is unusual, offer a short note and a call, and do not pretend a dropdown can capture the nuance. The dropdown will be wrong, and the person will feel classified. Leave an open field for the sentence only they can write. Read it.

Tables are the other place marketing sites ask people to compare without a conversation. [Tables on a marketing site](/blog/tables-on-a-marketing-site) is about rows that are real differences, not a grid of checks that are all checked. Read it when your form is honest and your pricing or comparison block is still a poster.

If you want to see interfaces where the questions are as considered as the layout, look at [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The useful test is whether you would be willing to fill the form yourself, on a phone, with one hand, while someone waited.
